speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that on October 12 we did indeed submit a formal note to the Secretary of State's department in the United States along the lines indicated by the hon. member and as reported over the weekend. speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GARRISON DIVERSION-UNITED STATES POSITION ON MORATORIUM ON CONSTRUCTION OF LONETREE RESERVOIR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think our posture is that we simply do not know if that is going to be the case. Because of the uncertainties, and because these cannot be resolved in the absence of the detailed report of the IJC, this is precisely why we requested the United States administration to refrain from any further construction. In other words, we are not clear, and I doubt very much if anyone can be specific at the moment, as to what impact the construction of Lonetree will produce. That is why we felt that a moratorium should be decided on by the United States pending completion of the IJC report, which I think hon. members are aware will not be completed, because of its complexity, until some time late in the spring of 1977.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief point of order with respect to a matter on which I should like your advice. It concerns the reply to my question No. 764 on the order paper, dated October 21,1976, and, specifically, part 9 of the reply. The question is brief and, I submit, quite clear. Part 9 reads as follows:
Was data derived from Statistics Canada sources sold or offered by the four employees or Alan Jefferys Associates to any other organization or individuals and, if so, (a) what data, (b) to whom, (c) what were the actual or proposed amounts of transactions?
Your Honour, since my question was clear, and the answer to it not complete, only stating that the RCMP investigation indicated that Alan Jefferys Associates produced studies for five other clients, apparently in order to provide complete details the order paper went on and listed some of these, but a key item was omitted. That answer ignored the essential word "offered" in my original query, thereby conveniently failing to deal with an integral part of the question. To this extent, the answer is misleading.
My point of order is simply to ask if Your Honour could possibly clarify, for my benefit and the benefit of other members of the House, whether it would be in order to request the minister to cause the answer to be enlarged so as to reflect more accurately the true situation, or whether it is within the rules of the House that answers which are not complete and which could be misleading can be put forward with impunity. I realize that the answer need not be given at all, but my submission is that if it is given, it ought to be reasonably complete. In view of the fact that I have placed more questions on the order paper today and there are a considerable number outstanding, I am bringing this matter to Your Honour's attention so that I may, hopefully, receive more accurate and complete answers to these questions in the future.

The House resumed from Wednesday, November 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that Bill C-19 is very much a bill about the style of this government. It is a bill about how far the government judges it must go in order to restore some measure of confidence among the people of the country. It is a bill which consists, it seems to me, in a large amount of vagary and, to use the current fashionable expression, it is a purely cosmetic operation. It is because of this sham, because of this posturing, that the government finds itself in deep trouble with the public of Canada, a matter that I think should worry us whether we sit on this side of the House or on the other.
Canadians do not mind shell games at some fall fair or agricultural exhibition. They are amused by the sleight-of-hand and the speed of the operator. They are prepared to lose a dollar or two as the game goes on. But they care very deeply if the sleight-of-hand is perpetrated by ministers of the Crown. If any bill has evidence of this, it is Bill C-19 which is one of the most interesting shell games outside an agricultural fair that I have ever seen. What has happened, of course, is that the columns of figures have been moved from one page of government ledger to another. In clause 15 the government notes that basically this part of the bill will affect people who do not have as much clout and who do not have as much power and cannot bring as much pressure to bear on the government as others. So the cosmetic operation continues.
Members of parliament on this side of the House are asked to buy this bill. I may say that if it had not been for the most eloquent and positive speech of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) last Wednesday, I do not think we would yet have heard the government's proposal which was given by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) about the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
When ministers move millions of dollars from one column of government ledgers to another, the public understanding, the public cynicism, the general malaise of the public of Canada is only accentuated. This is why I wanted to take a minute or two to discuss the bill and explain why 1 characterize it as a measure of the style of this government. It is a style which has effectively disillusioned the vast majority of Canadians who doubt the government's capacity for leading the country. Bill C-19 which we are now debating is, in the vernacular, the son of Bill C-87, with the same inherent defects. The government has brought the bill forward because it persists in its arrogant assumption that the people of Canada will swallow anything. That is partly why members of the opposition, in discharging their obligation to the people of Canada, must take a day or two debating a bill so patently phony in conception.
Let us talk about clause 1 5 of the bill which, as I said, seeks to repeal section 272 of the Railway Act. In the name of restraint the government sought to abolish the subsidy on the movement of grain and flour through the ports of Saint John and Halifax. Many members-I shall be more generous than the Minister of Transport-on both sides of the House reminded the government how serious the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act would be for those eastern Canadian ports. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax finally smoked out the government. As my colleague said on November 10, as reported on page 957 of Hansard:
Nothing can justify this-this thoughtlessness; perhaps I should not use the word "arrogant". Nothing can excuse this ineffectiveness and indecision .. . Unless the minister is prepared, right now, to disclose in some detail what he has in mind, this bill should no longer be debated at this time.
The hon. member for Halifax threw down the challenge, and 1 must compliment the government because the challenge was taken up; the big guns participated in the debate. Following the hon. member for Halifax, the Minister of Transport said, as reported at page 957 of Hansard:
When the earlier bill was on the order paper I stated it was our intention to do some serious work on the question of movement of grain and flour which could and should take place after the old section 272 of the Railway Act was no longer in existence.
I am prepared to congratulate the government for belatedly and reluctantly facing the facts, namely, that opposition to the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act made it impossible, and properly so, for the government to secure passage of Bill C-87 in the previous session. Such opposition threatens to delay the progress of Bill C-19 of the present session. Although I am not privy to all the secrets of the Minister of Transport, and 1 shall disclose one or two of his secrets in a minute or two, I think he will agree that the extensive criticism and debate of the previous session was not in vain for it brought about a deathbed repentance on the part of the government.
The minister, in his somewhat restricted vision, could only remind the House that the hon. members for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Douglas), South Western Nova (Miss Campbell), and Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Landers) were concerned about this bill. I prefer to take a more generous attitude than that of ministers

November 15, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
who think that nobody but government backbenchers could support such an important bill.
May I interpolate this: if the government had been more generous in accepting opposition suggestions and criticisms, its legislative program would have enjoyed easier passage in the House. As I say, I prefer to take a more generous attitude and would add the official opposition and New Democratic Party members to those who resisted the government's blandishments and its vague promises that it would work to see what the effects of amending the Railway Act would be. It is apparent that in the intervening months it did not do this work. In my opinion, such work should have preceded the introduction of Bill C-87. That is why I talked about the style of government.
I was fascinated to note that despite recommendations made to the government, despite suggestions made by government backbenchers and put on record by members of my party, the New Democratic Party and the Social Credit party about the serious effects on the economy of the deletion of this section in the Railway Act, the government paid no attention, as was evident when it introduced the bill. Months went by. The bill was introduced, but little progress was made. Then the bill was brought forward for debate. Finally, on November 10, 1976, after the hon. member for Halifax had challenged the government to put up or shut up, the Minister of Transport stepped out of his hangar, if 1 may put it that way, and with an attitude of "full ahead go", if I may use the expression, said action would be taken and that the Canadian Millers' Association had accepted a government proposal.
In a memorandum to the cabinet dated May 25, 1976, the following recommendations were made for cabinet approval. They involved, first, the introduction of a new program of assistance to the Canadian milling industry, based on a direct payment for all export flour shipments except aid and shipments to U.S. destinations equivalent to the benefits of "at and east" rates, the level of payment to be announced following discussion with the Canadian Millers' Association. Second, the initiation of an inquiry by the Canadian Transport Commission to establish the actual cost of "stop-off' for milling in transit purposes. Third, the announcement of the above initiatives before further progress was made with Bill C-87.
I will never know why the cabinet did not accept those recommendations until November 10. During the question period a member of the cabinet spoke of the efficiency of the public service, an observation with which I am happy to agree. Yet here was a memorandum prepared for the cabinet by senior civil servants and it had to wait until November 10 for acceptance. Apparently the government is riding roughshod not only over parliament but over advice given to it by senior public servants in the form of a memorandum. This, I believe, accounts for some of the cynicism abroad in this land.
If the government had accepted the sensible recommendations made to it, by now either Bill C-87 or its progeny, Bill C-19, might be the law of this land. It is reasonable to expect that if the government had followed the advice it got from the public service, or parliament, Bill C-87 would now be part of

the law on our statute books. But because that is not the government's style, because the government expects parliament and the public to take it on faith-and never before in our history has such faith been more fragile, because the government did not have faith in the advice of its public servants and did not follow the advice of parliament-it has found it difficult to secure quick passage for its legislation.
I say all this because hon. members opposite keep asking the opposition if it wants restraint. Mr. Speaker, the opposition wants it, but it wants some genuine, hard evidence to show that the government is concerned about restraint. Second, in the concept of the amendment to the Railway Act, the public wants evidence that the government wishes to keep viable the two large ice-free ports of Saint John and Halifax, wants to continue the movement of grain and wants those two ports to continue the movement of flour as has occurred in other years. As I say, this comment is made with a great amount of graciousness to the Minister of Transport, who was smoked out by the hon. member for Halifax, that all sides of the House wanted to get on with this legislation when the government's intentions were known.
I have another minute or two and I want to go back to the matter of faith. If I can be philosophical for a minute, faith is a concept that needs underpinning; it needs evidence to support it. This government keeps trying to bring down the faith of the Canadian people. It keeps saying it will do this, it will do that, and it will give certain undertakings. Then the government, because it does not take its own advice or the advice of its public service, makes it impossible for those of us who feel very deeply that faith is an essential component in the democratic process. We end up unable to have any faith in the government. In a way, we become accomplices to the cynicism that is abroad in this land. It is abroad largely because of the indecisiveness, rudderlessness, lack of leadership and Johnny-come-lately, cosmetic style of government that should, in my opinion, for the sake of Canada, go to the people for their opinion so that needed changes can be made.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly happy to enter the debate at this time, following the very eminent member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather). Outside the political context he and I usually agree. However, before getting to the substance of the matter I wish to take up a few of the points he mentioned. First, I do not believe the hon. member is serious in his suggestion that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) did not listen to or work on the difficulties with regard to reductions and subsidies under the Railway Act which had been provided to millers. He cannot be serious in suggesting that that decision was made in the House last Thursday after the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) spoke. If the hon. member had listened to or had read the minister's speech, he would have known that it was only on that day the minister received an indication from the millers
November 15, 1976

that the program which had been discussed and offered to them was workable and that their exports were secure.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: That is exactly the point I was making.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halifax was very opportunistic. I do not see anything wrong with that. The hon. member for Funday-Royal also wanted to take a bit of the credit. I agree that when they speak in the interest of the Atlantic provinces they should get some credit. However, I want to put on the record that the Minister of Transport had been discussing the problem with the millers for a long period of time.
What the hon. member for Fundy-Royal expounded on this afternoon proves that the government was correct in questioning the process by announcing, in Bill C-87 last year, some reduction in subsidies. What happened was that an alternative that apparently was more efficient in economic terms, in terms of marketing and in many other ways, was subsequently developed by the millers and the government. The hon. member for Fundy-Royal said that the government was acting by fakery or in a cosmetic manner. In fact, the hon. member confirmed that sometimes when a program has been in existence for a long time it should be looked at. For example, it is sometimes necessary to say that a subsidy which has been in effect for a period of years is being looked at, it may have to be reduced and we will discuss a more efficient way of dealing with the situation.
In dealing with this bill, the hon. member spoke about fakery and cosmetics. When he does that he is, in fact, saying that during the previous election campaign the Conservative party was engaging in fakery and cosmetics. They talked about the elimination of Information Canada. I do not recall any talk about the abolition of the Company of Young Canadians. However, they talked enough about government spending to lead people to believe that government spending is waste. If this bill is fakery, then the Tory platform for the past six or seven years is also fakery and cosmetics. They cannot have it both ways. I cannot let my honourable friend, and 1 use the word "honourable" in the best way, get away with the comment about fakery in government. I know where he stands with regard to public accountability and the honesty with which he deals with politics. However, he is part of the political game, like 1 am. He knows that to talk about fakery, in the terms he talked about it, is just an illusion.
I do not believe that ordinary people have an overwhelming faith in their government. Let us not forget how the British people defeated Winston Churchill as the last world war was ending. During the war it was easy to attract people and tell them they had to defend the country. Because of the adversary position of politics, the credibility of our public institutions is impaired. However, that is the price we have to pay for what I think is the best system in the world.

Take medicare, for example. People were paying for medical services before the act was passed. The difference now is that the cost is shared, instead of being borne by individuals, and that the administration is in the hands of the federal government and the provinces. Thus, if the intention is to make an honest comparison, the cost of medicare services should be left out.
The same holds true in the case of the Canada Assistance Plan. It is true that hospital insurance was in effect before the beginning of the last decade, but a tremendous increase in cost has taken place since then. This is not government expenditure in the true sense of the word; it is a transfer of funds from one part of the country to another, a re-channelling of resources for the purpose of ensuring greater equity.
Consider government participation in the Syncrude project. This expenditure was undertaken in the national interest in view of the uncertainty of future oil supplies. When some of the original investors pulled out, governments, both federal and provincial, bought equity in Syncrude to ensure that the project went ahead. I will come to the boondoggles later. But once the objective has been decided on, how are the mechanics of implementation working? One of our difficulties, as a western democracy, is that very often a worth-while objective can be "fausse"-the word is French-by the manner of administration. One thing of which 1 am certain is this: when we intervene in the economy, we should make very sure we intervene in areas which are productive economically, socially and culturally.
A great many people suggest that the channelling of funds through unemployment insurance is unproductive. I challenge that assertion today, as 1 have in the past. In an area like mine, it is an accepted fact of life that not everybody can be permanently employed. Many individuals have been brought up to accept the custom of working for only part of the year and staying home for the rest. These people receive unemployment insurance benefits. But the fact that they are, as it were, unemployed does not mean the funds they receive are being spent unproductively. It is part of a tradition that a lot of people repair their homes during that period. If they are fishermen, they repair their gear. If they are loggers, they repair their logging equipment. What happens in other levels of the economy? Similar repairs are made from time to time and the expense of doing so is included immediately in the cost of the product. So what is the difference if an individual
[Mr. Breau.)
carries them out in the course of the winter while receiving unemployment insurance benefits?
It seems to me that when we are talking about the percentage of the gross national product the government should take, we should bear in mind what I have said. Instead of being 30 per cent or 40 per cent, it could be 50 per cent and the process would still be productive. I do not believe it is necessarily bad when government intervenes, nor do I believe'that government should necessarily intervene. There are, of course, areas in which intervention is necessary. The arrangements under which federation was agreed upon do not, in any case, make economic sense. The present political fabric is a result of a series of deals made between various regions or economic areas to unite under a parliamentary form of government. In accordance with this overriding decision, one of the first things to be done was to direct the economic affairs of the country east-west. In my part of the country that does not make any sense at all, economically; but it was upon such considerations as these that confederation was made possible. The final result, however, was the emergence of a country in which there was a singular need for intervention at government level if the country was to flourish and survive.
I cannot complete my remarks on this subject without mentioning the hypocritical attitude adopted by some members, particularly those in the Conservative party, when they continue to blather about the evils of government intervention. It is nonsense to suggest that government intervention could be avoided in the context of the Canadian reality. Absence of such intervention would mean prosperity for only a few special areas; the rest of the country would face disaster and eventually confederation would break up. This becomes evident in other fields. What, for example, should be the response to inflation? The traditional response is to tighten up fiscal and monetary measures, a strategy which worked effectively in Japan. Some people say that it worked effectively in the United States. I am not so sure about that. It worked in economic terms, but I should like to study the social cost of having fought inflation by fiscal and monetary means in the United States. It worked in West Germany. I do not think it works in Canada.
Surely we do not have to start giving these kind of fundamental lessons on political economy in a House like this. The economy must serve the people first, not vice versa. The simple fact is that if you fought inflation, in the Canadian reality, with fiscal and monetary policies alone, you would have five provinces bearing the brunt of fighting inflation while the other five continued to produce and to prosper.
I mentioned the ambivalence or hypocrisy of some. If you read the speech of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal and others, they talk about the terrible effect of eliminating the subsidy under the Railway Act. They talk of the terrible effect of the stabilization act and say that payments will be delayed. They talk of the terrible effect of a few other things. On the other hand, whenever the president of some bank or some big

That is what I call ambivalence. Tory members speak of the necessity of intervention to provide grain stabilization, to stabilize prices and to give a subsidy to the millers, but the simple fact is that you need government intervention in the economy.

That was a year ago. Government policy as put forward in the Speech from the Throne is not that there should necessarily be less government intervention. What the government said was that we have to be more careful about the kind of intervention, that we should make sure that when we do intervene, we intervene in a productive way. That is precisely the point that I was making. I should like to give the House an example of what I mean. I believe that today and forever more this country is going to need a network of day-care centres, not only for social reasons but for economic reasons. 1 suggest this should be obvious to anyone unless they live in an area unlike mine and do not have to deal with the kind of welfare cases I get in my constituency office and here. The Economic Council of Canada, in its recent report, stated that somewhere between 1982 and 1985 there is going to be a shortage of productive labour in this country. The fact is that a lot of mothers and women today who could be productive have to stay home to look after the kids. It would make more economic sense, quite apart from the social value of this, for the federal government and the provinces to set up a network of day-care centres.
Another area of concern is unwed mothers. We must accept the fact that morality and behaviour have changed, whether we like it or not. We are not a church; we are a political body and are limited in the extent to which we can impose morality upon the people. While some members would like to do that, 1 do not think that we can. We have to respond to moral behaviour and the comportment of society.

A lot of marriages are breaking up and mothers and fathers are left with one or two children; or sometimes the whole family splits up. There has been a change in attitude and in the lives of people, and this is one further reason why we need government intervention. Lately I have come across case after case of marriage breakdown and either the father or the mother is really put in the position of being unproductive. They cannot work or hold a permanent, productive job precisely because there are no day-care centres in their community. This is why we need more government intervention; the economy of and benefit to the country demands it.
It seems to me that it is all right to question the means by which government intervenes, to say that there is too much bureaucracy, or that the return we get from the bureaucracy is not productive enough. But in this regard I should like to hear hon. members put forward ways in which the bureaucracy can be made more responsive and productive in the kind of society in which we live. I think this is a problem most western societies have to deal with. It is not a simple one; it is a very complicated and complex one. It may be okay in a certain area to say that the mechanics of implementation become too complex and complicated, that they are too much borne down by procedures, that we should eliminate them and start afresh. But it is illusory to talk about the dangers of too much government intervention, and in the Canadian context it would be a disaster, generally speaking, if government were to decide massively to reduce its intervention in the economy.

It is a policy which I will not support in this House of Commons. I believe, as we all do, that inflation has to be fought. I believe, also, in the concept that expenditures must be restrained. But surely we must look at the various areas of this country and see where expenditures need to be restrained and where they do not need to be restrained as much.
It is beyond my comprehension how any government can restrain expenditures in an area of the country which has an unemployment rate of 13.9 per cent. It is, in fact, positively cruel and inhuman for any government to apply a restraint policy equally across this country as though every section of it is the same. It may be a policy of restraint that is quite apt for provinces like Ontario, Alberta or Saskatchewan, perhaps, where there are now high employment figures, but it is not proper to apply it blindly to Newfoundland which has an unemployment rate of almost 14 per cent.

It is borrowing more than it should to keep some construction and some employment going in the province, while the other government, with unlimited resources, with the Bank of Canada in its captivity and with power over currency and credit, ignores our conditions and treats us in the same manner that it treats every other part of Canada.

They followed the example of the hon. gentleman who sits in the House now, the former premier of Saskatchewan. For provinces such as Newfoundland, with our low ratio of doctors, a large part of the expenditure for the first few years came from the government of Canada under the provisions of that plan. But now that is changing. Now we have to pay about 64 per cent of the cost of medicare. Along comes the government which instituted the plan and suggests they will put a ceiling on it.

Who could argue that hospital wages should not be improved, compared with what they were three or four years ago? So they want to leave hospital insurance to the provinces and they want to leave medicare to the provinces.

They put their ceiling on the plans, a ceiling which has no relationship to the cost which the provinces have to bear in operating hospital insurance and medicare for many years to come. The result will be that provinces such as Newfoundland will no longer be able to carry on even the services they now have, much less improve them. If these plans and schemes come into effect, the province of Newfoundland will not be able to maintain its present services because more and more of its budget will have to go into medicare and hospital insurance programs already in effect.
The government of Canada put a ceiling on post-secondary education expenditures. I believe they will permit an increase of up to 15 per cent a year. Last year, post-secondary education cost Newfoundland $1.6 million more than it would have if that arbitrary ceiling had not been imposed. If the federal government had met its original obligation, Newfoundland would have had $1.6 million for those programs. That is not calculated to help the disadvantaged provinces in providing proper post-secondary educational services to their people. So in every direction we look, whether government-to-person or government-to-government programs, the record of the government opposite is a sorry one, and it is getting sorrier every day.

Bill C-19 is entitled an act to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures. The very basis of the bill is the obligation of the government to restrain spending. In the days of inflation this is obviously a desirable and urgent objective, but the restraint must be applied in the right places in order not to destroy constructive efforts to expand production or cause great hardship to those who can bear it least. My colleagues have discussed the detailed provisions of the bill and 1 should like to deal with a related matter which is not covered by the bill itself, that is, the whole question of restraint in government spending in the area of defence.
The point I wish to emphasize is that restraint in connection with government expenditures on unnecessary defence installations should be given serious consideration. The tendency of nearly all modern governments-and not only governments but the press and some parts of the public-is to treat government expenditures on defence as sacrosanct, that is, touch everything else but do not touch defence expenditures. It is not a popular subject, but it is an important one. On the other hand, I suggest there is no more inflationary expenditure than that on defence. It produces no consumer goods and does not produce extra goods. As we have all observed, defence spending has a self-perpetuating tendency. Defence installations go on and defence alliances go on whether they are necessary or unnecessary. I think this is a subject which requires careful consideration.
In Canada, not only have we embarked already upon substantial expenditures for military purposes whose usefulness may be doubtful, but the former minister of national defence spoke triumphantly in this House about a year ago saying that his department was not to be subject to a ceiling on expenditures but was to be allowed an increased capital expenditure of 12 per cent per annum for five years. I suggest that was clearly inflationary.
The tendency is the past has been to make these expenditures taboo and not a subject for discussion. The Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence can examine the details, but in this chamber in the past, with the governments we have had, there has been no tendency to consult with that committee on the major projects that are contemplated. A notorious example is the purchase of the Orion, the LRPA, from the Lockheed Corporation. This was sprung on the Canadian people, with a minimum of discussion
Restraint of Government Expenditures about its basic purpose, at a price that turned out to be over $ 1 billion. There was a lot of discussion about the details and the ineptitude exhibited in handling the negotiations by the government which did not have a word in writing.
There has also been discussion throughout the world about the mismanagement in Lockheed and its worldwide system of bribery. I hasten to add, Mr. Speaker, that no one suggested any Canadian was bribed. It would appear that our defence department was ready to accept the advice of American officials with an interest in the financial stability of Lockheed without serious question. The fact is that the Orion had different purposes and roles. One major role assigned to it was participation in long-range and submarine warfare in the Atlantic. The scenario provided for an attack by superior conventional forces of the U.S.S.R. and Warsaw pact in Europe, followed by a protracted war in Europe in which the North American continent would seek to send supplies by ship to Europe. This method of supply would be countered by submarine warfare in the North Atlantic. It was proposed that long-range patrol aircraft could be used to fly across the Atlantic to detect and destroy submarines and thereby protect the sea lanes of the Atlantic.
The weakness of this scenario is that it is hardly credible. It is most unlikely that such a war would emerge in the missile age. Indeed, in the two great wars fought in the past the containment of the submarine menace was of the utmost importance, and strenuous measures were taken for dealing with submarines. It would be a grave mistake to transfer to the present day the thinking which applied to the totally different circumstances existing during those wars. It is hard to believe that if, as assumed, the U.S.S.R. were to launch even a partially successful attack on Europe, the war would not quickly develop into a nuclear war.
This situation has been foreseen. For example Air ViceMarshall Stewart Menaul, head of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence Studies, London, says that present NATO strategy means that only immediate use of nuclear weapons would stop a Warsaw pact assault. In the series called "Power at Sea," one of the Adelphi papers submitted by the institute of strategic studies-by Professor Hedley Bull who is well known in the field-analysed what small powers can do in naval warfare and recommended that their role should be the defence of coastal waters and fishing zones out to the anticipated 200-mile limit. By the same token, he gives reasons for thinking that extended submarine warfare is not a suitable role for the forces of a small or medium power. So far as Canada is concerned, preparation for this sort of submarine warfare is a waste of time and money. In addition, we are committed to spend some $184 million on German Leopard tanks which are to be used mostly in the central plains of Europe. If it is necessary for Canada to continue this role, perhaps that is a reasonable expenditure. In any event, that proposition, too, requires review either by parliament or the defence committee.

On the other hand. Bush said, the U.S. has many weapons systems that the Russians cannot duplicate.
That is enough to illustrate my point. It is not that these figures are necessarily correct. They may well be wrong. It is not that we should close our eyes, drop our guard, or any other expression you want to use with regard to a careful study of what is required-an awareness. We live in a world that could turn very hostile. Therefore, I am not asking that that be done. What I am asking is that we do not rush into every heavy expenditure proposed by certain defence sources merely because of some panic created about what is supposed to be the situation in the U.S.S.R.
I conclude by making an appeal to the House, especially the Minister of National Defence, to start a new era in this matter of defence spending, an era in which the policies of the government shall be open. 1 know there are secrets that cannot be divulged, secrets that have military significance. However, the over-all purpose and the over-all role we have to play can well be discussed by intelligent people. There is a lot of expertise required in this field. People who know what they are talking about have often stated that intelligent people directing their minds to these matters can come up with rational, common sense and worth while conclusions. We in this House have not been given the opportunity to do so.
I hope the new Minister of National Defence will usher in a new era, partly through the committee and partly through statements in this House. I hope he will make sure that what we do is needed to be done, that the people of Canada understand why it is being done and, if it is not necessary, the restraint which we urge in other fields will be applied in this field as well.

I should like to take a few moments to discuss one of the clauses of Bill C-19 which has to do with family allowances. Instead of being negative, perhaps one of the speakers for the Conservative party would like to comment on the question whether the government should be tying family allowances in with family income; in other words, whether a family with an income of $50,000 a year or more should be getting a family allowance amounting to $22 or $23, or whatever it is, as opposed to a family with an income of around $7,000 a year.
We have set precedents in the past under the old age pension program and other government programs. We recognize that some people have less money than others, and we say to them, "When it comes to federal funding, we shall place the main emphasis on the needs of those with lower incomes." We do not give equivalent grants of money to those who have been successful in life. Rather, we have concentrated on those who, in many cases through no fault of their own, have lost the ability to make the same kind of income as more fortunate citizens enjoy.
What does the official opposition say about this? It would obviously be possible to save money by withdrawing the allowance from high income earners and redistributing it among families which are finding real difficulty in meeting the burden of inflation, families in which the breadwinner might have serious problems about holding a job in present economic circumstances. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether it would not be better for us to address ourselves to this problem rather than to the question whether the $22 should be frozen or not. Speaking for myself, 1 have some doubt as to whether this money is being directed to those who most require it.
We all know that the costs of raising a family have increased tremendously in the last few years. Young people starting out in marriage today often decide that both shall work for the first five or ten years, not because the wife particularly wants to go out to work, or because the husband wants to come home and cook TV dinners, but because it is very costly to bring up a family during times of inflation. If we accept this situation, should we not be asking ourselves, as members of parliament, whether the many millions of dollars

which go out in the form of family allowances are going to the right people? Never before has there been such a consistently uniform expression to all members of parliament by their electorate as on the issue of capital punishment. For about the past five years every reliable indicator has shown that about 80 per cent of the Canadian people wanted to see a return of the death penalty. The Liberal government achieved the majority vote it sought on that issue by using the age-old tactic of the decoy and thereby fragment the opposition. The Liberal cabinet voted as a block and were, in fact, expected to show solidarity behind a government-sponsored bill; but each other member of the House, on the surface at least, was supposed to vote independently. This gave the government not only the advantage of an immediate block of about 28 votes but also the influence of that block for persuading others.
The decoy strategy centred on promoting the idea of a "free" vote or "conscience" vote, incidentally thereby absurdly implying that none of the other votes taken in parliament are either "free" or "conscience" votes. In my mind, Mr. Speaker, this is what has destroyed the respect Canadians ought to have for the institution and the elected members who make up this body. It is this superseding of private wishes over the wishes of the Canadian people that is making every thinking and feeling elector distrust all those men and women who run for public office.
I can well imagine that during the 1974 election every member of this House, in one way or another, said to their electorates, "Vote for me; I want to be your representative in Ottawa". Two years later they had their greatest chance. They were faced with a vote that was openly non-partisan, a vote that gave them the clear opportunity to represent the wishes of their constituents without any prior commitment to any party policy. Every member was aware of the numerous national polls on this subject; probably all members had approximately the same ratio indicated in their mail when the public was speaking out on this issue. The government, faced with this reality, had to find some way to defeat the will of the majority. They found it by declaring that the vote on capital punishment would be a "conscience" vote, again implying that members do not exercise their conscience on any other votes.
So the debate on capital punishment as a subject itself was really an exercise of diminishing importance, except for the very important factor of providing the electors with information on how each member established his position and justified his vote. In the end, the vote was really not on capital punishment as much as it was a test of whether or not parliament was an expression of the will of the people. Clearly, we failed. We failed because all of us, to one degree or another, bought the validity of the concept of the free vote. Faced with the choice of representing their electors or representing themselves, many chose to represent themselves.
1 said during the debate that such a response was nothing but elitism. It is, in effect, saying that regardless of what the majority of Canadians think on this issue, and regardless of how definitively they have expressed themselves on it, the members here know better and, therefore, can override the will of the majority. I am not forgetting, Mr. Speaker, that sometimes this is the case, that it is in fact the job of the member to study issues in detail, to use all the resources at his disposal, resources that may not be available to the general public, and then as a result perhaps arrive at conclusions that are unpopular and possibly misunderstood. But the issue of capital pun-
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment ishment has been the most talked about, the most studied, and the most thought-out issue by the public in recent years. The public was not uninformed or unthinking on this issue.
Is it not curious, Mr. Speaker, that when the Liberal government were elected in 1974, they took pride in how intelligent and insightful the electors were in choosing them to govern, yet within two years they were saying that those same electors, who two years previously were so smart, were now so dumb they could not be trusted with such an issue. 1 think the public now knows it has been used, that it has been had. Is it any wonder we face a problem of voter apathy in this country? Too many voters have been convinced by such decisions as this one, isolated from the will of the voting public, that such candidates and members of parliament come to them only out of necessity at election time. Such actions by parliament have convinced voters that their vote will have no real effect on the destiny of Canada.
I know that those who disagree with what I am saying will counter by saying, in effect, "What do you want a member of parliament to be, an automaton, slavishly repeating what he has been told by a partially or ill-informed public? Are we to have parliament made up of a delegate system, where members go home to a committee to receive instructions as to how they should vote, making parliament a kind of council of supreme Soviets, or presidium or, at best, a convention? Not at all; that is nothing but argument by the ridiculous; and the Canadian people don't expect that: they expect members of this House to be capable of intelligent and independent decision-making. But they also expect to be listened to and to be heard, and heard in earnest. Also, they expect honesty at election time. If candidates and members plan to ignore or disregard the will of their electors once they are elected, they should be honest enough to say so at the time.
If ignoring the will of the majority can be justified in any way at all, then why, pray, go through the expense and ritual of redistribution? Why enlarge the scale of possibilities to disillusion the electorate? This House seems to be perfectly capable of acting autocratically with its present size. Presumably we plan to enlarge the House to give better representation to the Canadian people. Presumably the additional members will permit all of us to get closer to the people and thereby get a better indication of the wishes of the people. But, Mr. Speaker, with this kind of rationale, all the increased size of the House will provide is an increased number of opportunities to disillusion our people.
For the past two years members of the cabinet have been travelling across Canada trying to get a consensus from various sectors of our economy. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has been seeking this for the government's antiinflation program. The former minister of finance met with groups of business leaders all across Canada trying to enlist them in a voluntary restraint program. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) has been seeking the same kind of co-operation from labour leaders.
No one would agree that this is not important or that the approach is not a useful one. But why does the government

take this approach only on economic issues? Why not get a much broader consensus on so-called moral issues? There is precedent for it. The Mackenzie King government had a referendum on the issue of conscription during World War 11. It could be done again on this issue.
I do not think anyone wants to see government by referendum. Members of this House have been elected to be decisionmakers. But on this issue 1 believe parliament has won the distrust of the Canadian people by disregarding their wishes. 1 see no other way to restore the confidence of the people that parliament deserves. 1 see no other way but to give them a direct and personal voice on this decision. Let them decide by referendum. This will relieve parliament of the onerous burden it now bears. If the people vote in favour of the death penalty, they will also carry the responsibility. If they reject it, they join themselves to the present decision. Either way, they will at least know that the will of the majority rules.
One last point, Mr. Speaker. In a democracy it is easy to be caught up with the notion that the majority is right. It may be, but not necessarily. In fact, in some cases it is probably not. "Broad is the road that leads to destruction and many there be that go in thereat". As a matter of fact, the majority of the world is now under totalitarian rule, but does that make it right? Obviously not. While we must always be concerned with the rightness of issues, and wrestle with them in a democracy and make our individual decisions on the basis of what we think is right, it is the majority which rules, not the rightness of the majority. And the majority has the right even to be wrong. Obviously the majority exercised that right at the last election.
In my maiden speech in this House just over two years ago 1 referred to the statement and the concern of John Stuart Mill, that great Liberal member of the British House of Commons 100 years ago. Always concerned that government should always be sensitive to the rights and feelings of minority groups, he spoke out strongly about the tyranny of the majority. But on the vote on capital punishment this concern has been reversed. We must now worry about the tyranny of the minority over the majority. It is time that the so-called "conscience" vote of the members was transferred to the collective conscience of the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the people of Canada deserve to have, and must have, confidence in parliament. They have lost it. I believe a referendum on this issue at the next election would go a long way to restoring that confidence. I trust the government will give the people that opportunity. I believe it is fortuitous that the one who will respond to this motion is the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee) who also voted in favour of capital punishment and who, therefore, I believe will support me in this motion.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED HOLDING OF NATIONAL REFERENDUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I say that I am very happy the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) introduced this

motion, because there was an explosive situation threatening this House and I hope we will take drastic measures this afternoon to overcome the crisis.
I think I should explain why I am speaking this afternoon and the context in which ! do so. Indeed I have taken part in the deliberations of the Committee on Procedure and Organization when it was considering the matter pf parliamentary reform. I then said that since the procedure followed for private members' business, was so outdated, I had decided that as long as the House did not accept to amend this procedure, I would participate as little as possible in the private members' business hour.
As a matter of fact, I think 1 must now correct this statement a little. I intend to stick to my remarks about bills introduced during private members' business hour, special business reserved to members, and I think that in the case of notices of motions, as the one introduced by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock, the situation is somewhat different and that the procedure such as it is, with all its faults, is valuable for these motions. When it comes to bills, though, I think that to make this hour really meaningful, the amendment proposed by the Committee on Procedure and Organization should be passed by the House.
This aside being over, I would like now to concentrate on the contents of this motion which, under a rather naive, even oversimplistic appearance, is in my view a real menace for our institutions and more particularly our electoral process. In fact if one cannot object to the idea of a referendum to find out and probe the majority opinion on this issue, I still think that the framework within which this motion is presented is a serious danger. I shall return to this point shortly when I draw a parallel with the present Quebec situation, in which, with the polarisation of votes, as far as a referendum is concerned, we end up by distorting the electoral process, that is the fundamentals of our institutions.
As far as the contents of the motion is concerned, as I said previously, 1 have nothing against it. It amounts to going directly to the people to find out what they think about the death penalty. As far as I am concerned, as far as my party is concerned, I do not share the same preoccupations as the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen). I think and I hope that the House has solved this problem once for all. We are the representatives elected by the population. I think we have the responsibility to act on behalf of the population, when the need arises. We do so each day in the House, especially on the questions which are debated here, as finances, consumption, the protection of the consumer, justice. By the way, we acted similarly as far as the death penalty was concerned and, again, I say I do not make the same reservations as the hon. member when he said that the decision that the House took on the subject of the death penalty was almost an abdication in the face of undue pressure from inside or outside. I think most hon. members took the decision in their own conscience, taking into account the pros and cons and I for one accept this decision, whichever way I voted on that question.
November 15, 1976

Consequently, the hon. member wants to leave it to the citizens for them to decide, for them to reverse the decision of the House, if they really decide to reverse it, for them to overrule the elected government, for them to take the place of their own members of parliament, in order to take an extremely serious decision, with multiple consequences, as human lives are at stake, and, without willing to come back on the substance of a very long debate we had in the House on that question, I will say once again that, as far as I am concerned, this question has been solved, members of all parties have presented their arguments to each other during the debate. 1 think that everything has been said on this subject and there is no need to start again an extremely emotional debate on the death penalty.
This being said, I am not opposed to the motion of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock on a matter of substance but rather on a matter of form because it is the form of the motion that is dangerous in these circumstances. Let us read it again. It is important! The hon. member proposes:
That in the opinion of this House the government should consider holding a national referendum for the purpose of making a survey of public opinion on the issue of capital punishment at the time of the next federal election.
There are two extremely important words, "national referendum" and there is also the words "at the time of the next federal election". Let us talk first about the referendum. Canada has never made it a tradition to hold referendums. Certain societies, certain systems are used to this practice of referendums but it necessitate a high degree of discipline, that we be highly accustomed to the process of referendums, that the population be very mature, and as this system has not been used regularly in Canada, 1 do not think it would be appropriate to use such a dangerous tool, because a referendum is very dangerous, it can divide the population into two clans, two factions, and afterwards it is extremely difficult to heal the wounds.
So I do not think that in our system the technique of referendum should be used to settle once and for all such a fundamental, emotive and personal problem as capital punishment is. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the capital punishment issue is one that is settled here, within one's heart; this is not something which can be reasoned. One has to weigh the pros and cons and decide whether he is prepared or not to sacrifice a human life for such and such reason. Some say yes, and I respect their opinion. Some say no. I am one of them, and I also think that this opinion should be respected by those in the opposite faction.
But if this debate is transferred to the public place, I can imagine what will happen. We will see the professional opinion makers come and go across the country with petitions, buy full pages in newspapers, and try to fill the debate with emotion. And how can you expect an individual who has certainly other things to do to examine all possibilities and choose among other alternatives, how can you expect him to come up with an enlightened decision on a situation such as this, when he is the object of conflicting opinions and excessive advertisement.
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment Again, there is evidence of this in other jurisdictions, whenever there is a referendum-and I am referring here to the entry of Great Britain in the European Common Market-there is absolutely unheard of propaganda from both sides.
How can you expect an individual to come up with an enlightened decision when he is the object, as undoubtedly he will be, with conflicting opinions? 1 put myself in his place and I say that this is impossible. Of course, under the present circumstances and in view of his own perception of events, with bloody titles published every day in newspapers and broadcasted by the news media, which, as a matter of fact, are to be blamed for stirring the emotions of the public. How anyone, Mr. Speaker, can expect the individuals concerned to reach an enlightened decision is beyond me.
The hon. member alluded to some statistics a while ago. I could quote him others, but it is a fact, I believe, that in the present situation, according to the information at our disposal, the majority of the people seem to be in favour of capital punishment. That is true. Let us admit it. Let us admit as well that we may not necessarily have all the facts. Now, what is a referendum? It is a two-edged sword.
If they are informed, they are enlightened; and if they are too well informed, they are completely lost. When one does not have the experience of the principle of the referendum, of the instrument it is, one does not realize it is a means to feel the pulse of the people. Without that experience, and, on such a touchy subject as that one, it is inadvisable to experiment, and that is what the hon. member would have us do, experiment. Let's go ahead and have a national referendum, a widespread debate on capital punishment! Mr. Speaker, I am not ready to tackle that adventure. And why not? I shall tell you right away. The idea of a referendum is not new. In Quebec, we know what referendums are because some people have been talking about them for six years now.
And to come back to the fact that the hon. member would have us hold a referendum on the occasion of a general election. Can you imagine that? The hodge-podge the Canadian people would have to face if a referendum on capital punishment were to be added to a federal election? How could we hold an intelligent election when every time problems, financial, economic or, as I mentioned a while ago, environmental, or anything else for that matter are approached, capital punishment would hold the center of the stage and its pros and cons be brought up again. How can an election be held under such circumstances? It is impossible.
It is impossible to hold a referendum at a federal election. I see that the hon. member opposite is smiling. It is true that I insist on a matter of form, but it is precisely this point which concerns me in his motion. Thus, each member would run for election and try to advocate, in the case of the official opposition, an alternative to the government program and, in the case of the government members, to defend the plans already implemented and all of a sudden capital punishment would be back on the floor. Each time we would want to discuss an intelligent matter, all of a sudden people would talk again about capital punishment. Mr. Speaker, the issue of capital

November 15, 1976
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment punishment has been settled here in the House of Commons. That's it! And if the hon. member is not satisfied with the decision of the House, there is nothing which keeps him, given our actual system, from presenting a bill. Let him introduce his bill we will debate it once again since it has to be done. But let us not rely on a referendum during federal elections. It is not possible. We cannot do such things; we cannot proceed blindly, trying small experiments, new systems, approaches or mechanisms to consult Canadians and thus jeopardize our democratic institutions. I am definitely against that.
That is exactly what is now going on in the province of Quebec. There is one particular political party which recommends a certain option. This option, Mr. Speaker,-facts and figures prove it-is rejected by the majority of the population. What did this party do? It is very smart. They said: we are going to set aside for a while the fundamental option which is the very reason for the existence of our party. We will set it aside for a while and when the time comes to discuss it we will then proceed by referendum. So here we go for the referendum.
But what is happening practically? During the provincial election of 1970, of 1973 and even today, Mr. Speaker, every time they come back to the same thing-referendum. What is happening? The real concerns of Quebecers are shelved. Economic problems, consumer issues, problems relating to industry, fishing, transportation, all that, Mr. Speaker, is thrown to the basket because what is important is the referendum, the basic option: people voted in 1970, in 1973 and again in 1976 for or against that option.
Do you see the danger, Mr. Speaker, of putting an issue before the people, at the time of a federal, national or municipal or provincial election, and of telling the people: We have to hold a very serious election, but for the time being the election is not important, because we must find out if you are in favour or against such and such a thing. It is not an election according to our system, it is not a matter of voting for or against something.
We know what happened for instance-I was not born yet at the time-but 1 learned what happened during World War II regarding conscription. But what happened? The conscription issue divided the country, Mr. Speaker. Why? Because the people were asked to vote for or against conscription. What happened? A segment of the population and, in this case, once again a certain province of the Canadian Confederation said no, and because it was a majority decision, it resulted in strike and unrest among the population. There were arrests, there were conflicts and wounds, and it took a long time before they healed.
Mr. Speaker, a referendum is dangerous. I am not against it in principle, but we cannot throw it before the public and say: Let's try it and see what will happen. It is something that needs preparation, that cannot be improvised. It is serious, and when 22 million people, are involved, Mr. Speaker, experiments are out of the question. A referendum is dangerous but a referendum on the occasion of a general election is inadmissible. It is not even dangerous, it is inadmissible because it
(Mr. Lachance.]
completely distorts the system. And I want to insist again on this subject. I do not want any referendum but still less on the occasion of an election because then you have the situation we are witnessing in Quebec: People do not have any choice; they no longer vote for a party, they no longer vote for ideas, they vote for an option, Mr. Speaker.
And what happens over the years? In the case of the province of Quebec, this creates dissensions, factions, and the province can no longer operate with factions. And if factions are created in Canada on the basis of the results of such a referendum, or of one option, or another Mr. Speaker, there is no room for Canada in the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of rising in this debate, but certain things were said that I absolutely cannot leave unnoticed.
First of all, I congratulate the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) for giving us this opportunity to speak on the matter of the capital punishment. The hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) said earlier that the people had already forgotten all about that. I wish he knew how much the people have not forgotten. As an illustration, let the Progressive Conservatives come to power and bring forward capital punishment, and we will see how the liberals will lose on that issue. They forced abolition upon this House. They found a way so that the opinion of the minority could win in this House. This prime minister (Mr. Trudeau) moved heaven and earth to have his idea accepted because when he has something in mind, there is no way anyone can take it out. He tried four times-I was here every time-and the last one, when he saw he would not get a majority because some of his own supporters would not vote with him and had the courage to stand up, what did he do? He called for Cabinet solidarity. He forced all his ministers to follow him, some of them against their own wishes. He forced them to. We saw that, I do not have to give names because everyone knows them. He did not have a majority, he forced his will and everyone said the minority had won. Because 80 per cent of Canadians, as the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont rightly stated, favoured retention.
Each time the matter came up, I took polls in my constituency and others as well. Every time 80 per cent favoured capital punishment. But someone's mind was on abolition. The government had sworn to abolish capital punishment despite everything and everyone else. And so they did. We asked for a referendum, and like the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont I feel that a referendum as part of a general election, is manipulating both the election and the referendum.
You have the same thing, the same result as in today's Quebec election. Mr. Bourassa's election issue is the patriation of the constitution, and look what happens: Mr. Bourassa's administration is entirely forgotten; all the other parties were trying to put that subject back into discussion and they did, so that Mr. Bourassa has completely lost face. The people wanted to discuss his administration.
November 15, 1976

Come election time that is what ought to be discussed, the administration of the government in power, in order to point to the good aspects, if any, and denounce the bad ones. There is always something good or bad in any government. I have no worry in that respect. Having to vote against a motion like the one before us is an impossible task. It would be defeated because I do not want capital punishment or issues as serious as that to become the issue of an election when an election should mainly deal with economic issues. An issue like that must be deal with individually, separately, through a referendum only. The hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) suggested that it is such a personal question that it must not be interfered with. It is up to everyone's judgment. That is why I always blamed the government for going against the judgment of the majority of the people. And it is all very well to say that the people are too ignorant but, Mr. Speaker, the heart, as the hon. member suggested earlier, cannot be ignored.
It is all very well to apologize for voting against capital punishment because the general public was uninformed. I do not accept that. 1 did not say so, the hon. member who spoke before me said so when he suggested that it was a matter of feeling. The feeling was too strong. It was a personal question. That is why we must go to the people and ask for their assent. And as we say in democracy, if one really want to be democratic .. . Furthermore, 1 always considered that this government could not care less about democracy in all its actions either with the provinces or with associations. If you want to be democratic you start by meeting the wishes of the majority of the people on capital issues. And then the people will start saying that you are being democratic and that you want to remain so. That is why I am and I have always been in favour of a referendum on that issue, and I will always be. The day a government decides to be honest by calling a referendum on that issue, 1 will start to take it seriously.
We saw what happened in the United States. It was said that it was settled and dealt with. Other U.S. states restored it; they had abolished capital punishment and they were forced to reinstate it. You will see that the French-Canadians in a few years will be forced to restore it, as will the Canadian government. Let us wait and see who is right. But that will never stop me from speaking for the people on those issues, and as long as they express the wish to have a referendum on that issue, whether for or against, 1 will follow the thinking of the majority of the people. Those are the few comments 1 wanted to make and I am sure that even if this hour ends inconclusively as all the others we will still have the opportunity to discuss that question later.

speechtext:
I am not rising to speak on the subject of capital punishment. We have expressed our views on that in this parliament; a vote has been taken, and I have no desire to challenge that here. [DOT]! find it hard to understand that hon. members could rise in this House and urge us to change our whole parliamentary system merely because they are not satisfied with a particular vote. But this is somewhat easier to understand when we consider the confusion which is latent in the motion as introduced by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock. 1 must draw the attention of the House to the words of the motion, which are as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider holding a national referendum for the purpose of making a survey of public opinion on the issue of capital punishment at the time of the next federal election.
In the language of political science the word "referendum" has reference to a binding expression of national opinion. You can clearly see that the author of this motion does not have that concept in mind. He uses the word referendum where he should use the word "plebiscite", which is a non-binding expression of national opinion. Worse than that, and this gives an indication of the kind of problem that can arise, we do not have the mechanism in our system to make a referendum legally binding. If we were to have a referendum, it would have to be followed by an act of parliament, with the members of parliament being bound by the referendum not having the right to vote independently on the issue. In effect they would be bound by something that happened outside this House, and that would be destructive of the whole parliamentary tradition.
In those places where they have referenda they are part of the constitution, and the free vote of the electors itself changes the law. They do not have a subsequent vote by the state assemblies in the United States to ratify what the voters have done by the referendum. The voters do it by vote. But that is a different system.
What I find most astonishing is that this innovation which our friends would introduce is the type of thing that they would decry in other circumstances. They are the first party to complain about any departure from the British tradition, and yet they are trying to introduce an aspect of the American system which would have the effect of entirely vitiating the system we hold so dear.
I repeat that the issue before us this afternoon is not capital punishment. I can appreciate that feelings on capital punish-

November 15, 1976
Public Opinion on Capital Punishment ment are strong in the country. Feelings are always strong on moral issues. Why have a referendum on this one moral issue? Are we going to have another one on abortion? We could hardly distinguish between these questions. If the hon. member were to say the distinction would be based on the precondition of a free vote, I would point out that his system would replace the vote entirely. Then do we have a referendum on the questions of divorce, of gun control- where do we stop? If we were to introduce a device of this kind we would be in a position where at least all issues of moral content, in the generally accepted sense of the word, would have to be submitted to the vote of the people. There is no possibility of isolating a single vote of this kind and treating it as something separate.
It seems to me that in our system the only case in which a referendum could be justified would be one dealing with the system itself. There are various ways of changing the constitution. If what we are talking about is something which is in effect a change in our system, if it is like the vote in Great Britain on entering the Common Market, which is a limitation on the sovereignty of parliament and does change the course of British history, then perhaps there is a case for it. If we had a similar case here which was changing our future course, or a vital question dealing with the government itself, that would be different, but if we are dealing with ordinary moral issues they are all on the same plane. While some people are concerned about capital punishment, others are concerned about abortion. Sometimes they are the same people, and sometimes separate groups, but one group has as much right to have its issue put to a national referendum as another. In my view no group has that right in a parliamentary system.
I do not have to explain to hon. members opposite the historical genesis of parliamentary government and how we fought for it in Canada with the result we see in the party caucuses. We were the self-governing dominion in the British Commonwealth which developed the party caucus because we were all united against the governor. The higher-ups in all parties met with the ordinary representatives because they were all together in their struggle against the governor. From that arose our caucus, which has few parallels in the world, where frontbenchers and backbenchers meet together. It functions very effectively in our system-almost all of our system is functioning very effectively, or it was until our friend, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock, got into it.
I appreciate the fact that hon. members opposite, not having the responsibilities of office, do not have to be responsible in the motions they put forward, but on this side we have to take the longer view, especially when it is a question of responsible government itself.
I can see that this debate is provoking great concern in the House. Members on both sides would not want to lose the privileges they have attained through centuries of struggle for responsible government. Even members opposite, as a result of the things that are being said, may be persuaded to reconsider this thoughtless and unwarranted suggestion that in one aspect would change our system in a way that could drive a wedge that would eventually change its character entirely and run the

risk of creating in Canada, or importing, the kind of institutions that have been developed in the United States.
I am sure most hon. members know, and certainly those on this side do, that there is a considerable difference between the spirit of the people and the spirit of government in Canada and the United States. We have a more relaxed notion of freedom and a different concept of government. We do not believe that everything should be put to a popular vote all the time. We think representatives should be elected to make decisions for the people on an orderly basis, themselves responsible to the people and the government responsible to them, so that throughout the system there is a chain of responsibility.
The American system is different. They believe in what many would refer to as an excessive democracy-that everything should be decided by everybody all the time. It is in that kind of spirit that referenda came to be part of the American system but I do not think it is a characteristic we would like to duplicate. There may be some things for which we envy our friends, such as their more material achievements, but I do not think members of this House want to ape their governmental institutions.
